meta.title: Five Shapes, One Neck
meta.summary: Every overlap between neighbouring A-minor windows holds a complete 1 b3 5 on three adjacent strings, so there is nowhere on the neck where an Am chord isn't under your hand.

spans.text: Five forms, five windows. Here they are side by side.
The same five, with where their roots sit and how you'd actually reach for them.

spans.text: Look at the pattern in that second table. Two forms — A and E — you can play start to finish, barre and all: the open
Am

and the fret-5 barre, the two the opener handed you for free. The other three live in pieces, and every fragment worth reaching for out of them has already turned up in this chapter — none of it is new here.
One more table, and it's the one this whole chapter has been building toward: where the
b3
sits inside each grip — the note you can put a finger on, without counting, to know a shape is minor rather than major.
One Neck, No Gaps
Now the whole neck at once, in roots. Two ladders, back to back.
Look closely and the two are identical. Same five bands, same frets, same roots lit — the only thing that changes is the caption. That's not the component being lazy; it's
the window stays, the third moves

, made in a single picture instead of in words. A window is anchored on the root, and the root never moved when the quality did. (One reminder, since it's easy to go looking: the ladder marks roots only. There's no
b3
to find on it — the tables above are where that lives.)
Now look at where neighbouring windows overlap, because that's where the last piece falls into place.
Every one of those four seams holds a complete
on three adjacent strings — nothing to stretch for, in any of them. Two you have already met: the first is the fretted part of the open
Am
, and the second is the one-finger grip at fret
. No two of the four are quite the same fret pattern, though — three of them cross the
G → B

break, where standard tuning's one major third shifts everything a fret, and they don't all sit in the same inversion either. What they share is the part that matters: three strings, a whole chord, no stretch.
You are never between forms. Wherever your hand lands on this neck, the notes under it belong to two windows at once, and there's a whole
Am
sitting right there.
Everything repeats at fret 12, the same as it does in major. The A form comes back as a barre there —
— and the ladder above wraps exactly the way it looks like it's about to.
Play that barre at fret 12 and it's the same
Am

you played open, an octave up, the same finger doing the same job on the same string. Nothing about the shape or the reasoning changes; the neck just runs out of new territory and starts giving you the first five windows again.
The same five windows carry the next layer too. Chapter 3 adds the
and the
b7
to each one — no new shape is ever asked for.
